div.head: Ps Cn for 4
div.ab: Sub horum iterum quolibet sint duo minutorum hominum, quos tunman Angli dicunt; hii nocturnam curam et ueneris et uiridis tum seruilia opera subibunt.
div.note: New row (October 2026): Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 621 (two independent readings of the page images, differences settled against the page)
div.ab: Under each of these again let there be two of the lesser men, whom the English call tunman (townsman, villager); these shall undertake the night-time care both of the venison and of the vert, and also servile works.

note.seg: tiefer als die II seruientes S. 620g, die eher Viridarii scheinen, sind hier Wald- und Wildhüter gemeint, die forestarii hiessen
Lower than the II seruientes on p. 620 (n. g), who seem rather to be Viridarii, what are meant here are keepers of the wood and of the game, who were called forestarii.
tunman übersetzt uillanus (s. u. 15) auch sonst; Maitland Domesday 59. Vom populus minutus sprechen Pipe roll a. 1130 p. 71; Ass. de Clarendon a. 1166, 20
tunman translates uillanus (see below, 15) elsewhere too; Maitland, Domesday 59. The Pipe roll of 1130, p. 71, and the Ass. de Clarendon of 1166, 20, speak of the populus minutus.

Minuti homines, meint Maitland Coll. papers II 102, hiessen Englisch smalemanni, die wie jene in Nordengland als Stand vorkommen. Allein halbfreie Bauern oder gar Unfreie, wie hier, scheinen jene nirgends. Vgl. Gl Bauer 1d. e

Minuti homines, Maitland thinks (Coll. papers II 102), were called in English smalemanni, who, like the former, occur as a rank in northern England. But nowhere do these appear to be half-free peasants, or even unfree men, as here. Cf. Gl Bauer 1d. e
